title: The Queen's Two Graves: Cameliard to Glastonbury, and the Northern Reckoning at Meigle
years: c. AD 495-1191 (a legendary lifetime, closed by the historical rediscovery of her grave)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cameliard, the court of Leodegrance
stops.campa: In the western march called Cameliard, King Leodegrance keeps a court whose chief treasure is not gold, and in it a daughter grows whose beauty later chroniclers will not tire of praising. Since Uther Pendragon's day the king has guarded a great round board of oak, a hundred and fifty places cut for as many knights, waiting for the hand that will complete its fellowship. Guinevere is raised among its empty seats, taught the courtesies of a hall built for equals, not knowing that her own marriage will carry the Table out of her father's keeping and into the world's memory.
suggested_refs: The Round Table of Leodegrance, ancestor of the table later kept at Winchester Castle
sources: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book III, ch. 1
Vulgate Cycle, Estoire de Merlin (Carohaise of Carmelide)
en.wikipedia.org, 'Carhaix-Plouguer' (Carohaise of King Leodegrance)

stops.name: The wedding at Camelot, and the gift of the Round Table
stops.campa: Merlin comes to Cameliard for Arthur and asks Leodegrance for his daughter. The old king answers that it is the best tidings he ever heard, and that he will send with her a gift dearer than land: the Round Table Uther once gave him, complete at a hundred and fifty sieges, and a hundred knights of his own, for fifty have been slain in his days. Guinevere rides out with Merlin, by water and by land in great royalty, until they come nigh unto London, and she is wedded to Arthur at Camelot in the church of Saint Stephen's, the Table set up behind her, its empty chairs still waiting.
stops.quote: I shall give him the Table Round, the which Uther Pendragon gave me, and when it is full complete, there is an hundred knights and fifty.
stops.quote_source: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book III, ch. 1
suggested_refs: The Round Table at Winchester Castle, painted Tudor replica of the legendary table
Caerleon's Roman amphitheatre, popularly called 'Arthur's Round Table'
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book III, ch. 1 and ch. 5
Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book IX

stops.name: Camelot, the fellowship sworn
stops.campa: At the high feast of Pentecost the young knights kneel around the Table and swear the oath Arthur sets them: to do no outrage and no murder, to flee treason, to give mercy to whoever asks it, to succour ladies, damosels and gentlewomen upon pain of death, and never to take up battle in a wrongful quarrel. Guinevere sits crowned beside her husband as the vow is renewed year on year, the hall's true mistress, the one whose name the fellowship will invoke as often as Arthur's own when a knight rides out to prove himself worthy of a place at her table.
stops.quote: never to do outrageousity nor murder, and always to flee treason... and always to do ladies, damosels, and gentlewomen succour, upon pain of death
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book III, ch. 15 (the Pentecostal Oath)
suggested_refs: The Winchester Round Table, its painted names and Tudor rose
South Cadbury hillfort, Somerset, identified with Camelot since Leland's 1542 survey
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book III, ch. 15
John Leland, Itinerary (1542)
Leslie Alcock excavations, South Cadbury (1966-1970)

stops.name: Caerleon, the queen crowned apart
stops.campa: At Whitsuntide the City of the Legions fills for the crown-wearing, and Geoffrey's Britain keeps a rite the later romances forget. The queen is crowned apart. Her own archbishops and bishops conduct her, not to Arthur's church but to the Temple of Virgins, and four queens walk before her bearing four white doves as ancient custom requires, a retinue of women following after in open joy. Two courts sit that day, two churches, two crowns, and the feast is not complete until both are kept. Here Guinevere is no ornament of the king's table but a sovereignty running beside his.
stops.quote: On another part was the queen, dressed out in her richest ornaments, conducted by the archbishops and bishops to the Temple of Virgins; the four queens also of the kings last mentioned, bearing before her four white doves according to ancient custom; and after her there followed a retinue of women, making all imaginable demonstrations of joy.
stops.quote_source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book IX, ch. 13, trans. Aaron Thompson
suggested_refs: The Roman amphitheatre at Caerleon, popularly called 'Arthur's Round Table'
The Roman legionary fortress of Isca Augusta, Geoffrey's City of the Legions
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book IX, ch. 12-13
Aaron Thompson translation, Six Old English Chronicles
caerleon.net, 'Royal Pomp at Arthur's Coronation'

stops.name: Camelot, Lancelot's coming
stops.campa: Out of the lake-country of Gaul rides Lancelot du Lac, and from the day Arthur knights him he is bound first to the king and, by the custom of the age's greatest romance, no less to the queen he serves as her own knight. Guinevere receives his courtesy as her due and gives him, in turn, the favor that makes him unmatched in every tournament he enters for her sake. The court does not yet call it anything but chivalry: a queen's champion riding out in her colors, proving, joust after joust, that no shield in Christendom stands higher than hers.
suggested_refs: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, le Chevalier de la Charrette, illuminated manuscripts of the queen's champion
sources: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot (c. 1177-1181)
Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book VI

stops.name: Glastonbury, the marshes of the Summer Country
stops.campa: Melwas, king of the Summer Country, carries off Guinevere and brings her behind the reed-beds and river-braid of his stronghold at the Glass Town, where causeways vanish into marsh and no army can safely follow. Arthur searches a whole year before he hears she is there, then rouses the armies of Cornubia and Dibneria and lays siege to a place ringed by water on every side. The abduction is no rumor here, no allegory: Caradoc of Llancarfan sets it down as history, the earliest hand to write that a king's wife was taken and a king marched to get her back.
stops.quote: It was besieged by the tyrant Arthur with a countless multitude on account of his wife Gwenhwyfar, whom the aforesaid wicked king had violated and carried off, and brought there for protection
stops.quote_source: Caradoc of Llancarfan, Vita Gildae (Life of St Gildas), section 10, trans. Hugh Williams (1899)
suggested_refs: Glastonbury Tor rising over the Somerset Levels, the 'Isle of Glass'
Ruins of Glastonbury Abbey
sources: Caradoc of Llancarfan, Vita Sancti Gildae, sections 10-11
Hugh Williams, Two Lives of Gildas (Cymmrodorion Record Series, 1899)

stops.name: Glastonbury Abbey, the peace of Gildas
stops.campa: Before the marsh can be forced, the abbot of Glastonbury steps into the space between the contending armies with Gildas the Wise and his clergy beside him, unarmed, and in a peaceable manner advises Melwas, his own king, to restore the ravished lady. Melwas yields the queen; the two kings, reconciled, give the abbot many domains in thanks and promise before the brothers never to violate so sacred a place again. Guinevere returns to her husband unharmed by the telling, restored in peace and good will rather than by the sword, and Glastonbury keeps, from that day forward, a claim on her story that will not let go of it.
stops.quote: Accordingly, she who was to be restored, was restored in peace and good will.
stops.quote_source: Caradoc of Llancarfan, Vita Gildae, section 11, trans. Hugh Williams (1899)
suggested_refs: Glastonbury Abbey ruins, the Lady Chapel over the site of the Old Church
sources: Caradoc of Llancarfan, Vita Sancti Gildae, section 11
Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot (later reworking, Meleagant for Melwas)

stops.name: Camelot, the queen's champion
stops.campa: Years deepen what began as courtesy. Lancelot rides for no other favor, wears no color but hers into the lists, and returns each time to lay the day's honor at her feet, quietly, the way a vassal lays it before his lord. The court reads it as pageantry, the highest knight paying the highest lady her due, and for a long while pageantry is all it needs to be. Only Agravain and Mordred, watching too closely, begin to name in the hall's dim corners what everyone else has agreed, for the fellowship's sake, not to see.
suggested_refs: Dante Gabriel Rossetti and the Pre-Raphaelite paintings of Lancelot and Guinevere
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII
Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot

stops.name: Westminster, the poisoned apple
stops.campa: Guinevere makes a private dinner for four-and-twenty knights of the Table and sets out fruit, because Gawain loves apples and pears and everyone who feasts him knows it. Sir Pinel le Savage, who means to avenge Lamorak on Gawain, poisons one; Sir Patrise of Ireland takes it, swells till he bursts, and falls dead among them. Because the queen made the feast, the suspicion is hers. Mador de la Porte appeals her of treason and not one knight will stand for her; Bors consents only on condition; Lancelot comes at the hour's end and overthrows Mador. It is the first time she is condemned to the fire.
stops.quote: considering Queen Guenever made the feast and dinner, they all had suspicion unto her
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 3
suggested_refs: Westminster Hall, the surviving hall of the medieval palace where Malory sets Arthur's London court
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 3-8
La Mort le Roi Artu (Vulgate Cycle), the poisoned fruit episode

stops.name: Astolat, the red sleeve and the barge
stops.campa: At Astolat, which Malory names for Guildford, Lancelot lodges with Sir Bernard and, to ride the Winchester jousts unknown, does the one thing he has never done for any woman: he wears another's token, the red sleeve of Elaine le Blank. The queen hears of it and is past reason with him, and Bors pleads that he bore it only so that his own blood should not know him. Elaine, refused, dies of it, and comes down the river to Westminster in a barge with a letter still in her hand. Guinevere reads it, and blames him not for the love but for the coldness.
stops.quote: Ye might have shewed her some bounty and gentleness that might have preserved her life.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 20
suggested_refs: Guildford Castle, Surrey, on the site Malory identifies with Astolat
Tennyson's 'The Lady of Shalott' and the Pre-Raphaelite barge paintings
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 9-20
en.wikipedia.org, 'Astolat' (Malory's identification with Guildford)

stops.name: Westminster, the Maying and the Knight of the Cart
stops.campa: In the month of May the queen gives warning that she will ride a-Maying into the woods and fields beside Westminster, and takes ten knights of the Table with her, all clothed in green, silk or cloth, each with a lady behind him, and no armour in the company. Sir Meliagrance has watched for exactly this season and this absence: he falls on the party with twenty men of arms and a hundred archers. Her knights fight until they are cut to pieces, and she surrenders herself to save their lives, on the one condition that they stay beside her. Lancelot comes after her in a woodcutter's cart.
stops.quote: the month of May was come, when every lusty heart beginneth to blossom, and to bring forth fruit; for like as herbs and trees bring forth fruit and flourish in May, in like wise every lusty heart that is in any manner a lover, springeth and flourisheth in lusty deeds
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 25 (the May prologue to the Knight of the Cart)
suggested_refs: Chrétien de Troyes, Le Chevalier de la Charrette, the cart of shame that Malory's Lancelot rides without hesitating
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 25 and Book XIX, ch. 1-9
Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot (c. 1177-1181)

stops.name: Carlisle, accused and condemned to the fire
stops.campa: Agravain and Mordred hide twelve knights in a chamber of the Castle of Carlisle and take the queen and Lancelot together, and though he cuts his way out through the chamber door, Guinevere is taken. Arthur, bound by the law he himself upholds, cannot save her by his own hand: treason found in the deed admits no remedy but death, and the sentence the court itself swore to keep is the fire. She is led forth without the city and despoiled into her smock, to be burned before the fellowship whose oath she has broken, the same fellowship that once knelt to swear mercy in her name.
stops.quote: then the queen was led forth without Carlisle, and there she was despoiled into her smock
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, ch. 8
suggested_refs: Carlisle Castle, its Norman keep on the site of Malory's court
Illuminated manuscripts of Guinevere led to the stake, French Vulgate Mort Artu cycle
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, ch. 6-8
La Mort le Roi Artu (Vulgate Cycle)

stops.name: Carlisle, the rescue at the fire
stops.campa: Lancelot comes out of an ambush in the wood with his kinsmen and breaks the ring of armed men around the stake, cutting down knight after knight in the smoke and confusion, among them Gareth and Gaheris, unarmed and unrecognized in the crowd. He casts a kirtle and gown over her, sets her behind him on his own horse and rides for Joyous Gard, saving her life and, in the same stroke, making an enemy of Gawain that no peace will mend. What had been a private grief becomes a public war, and the fellowship the Round Table was built to hold together starts, from this hour, to come apart.
suggested_refs: Joyous Gard, Lancelot's castle, traditionally identified with Bamburgh or Alnwick
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, ch. 8-9

stops.name: Joyous Gard, the queen kept and the queen given back
stops.campa: Bamburgh on its rock above the North Sea is the castle Malory's readers call Joyous Gard, though he owns that some men say Alnwick instead. Here Lancelot keeps the queen as a noble knight should do, and here Arthur and Gawain lay siege to town and castle for fifteen weeks that neither side can win. It ends by letter and not by arms: the Pope sends down his bulls commanding peace, and Lancelot rides her back to Carlisle with a hundred knights in green velvet, every man holding a branch of olive, and gives her into her husband's hands unbeaten, her name defended aloud to the last.
stops.quote: and so he rode his way with the queen, as the French book saith, unto Joyous Gard, and there he kept her as a noble knight should do
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, ch. 8
suggested_refs: Bamburgh Castle, Northumberland, named by Malory as Joyous Gard
Alnwick Castle, the rival claimant to Joyous Gard
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, ch. 8, ch. 10-15
La Mort le Roi Artu (Vulgate Cycle)

segments.name: The Fall of the Round Table

stops.name: The Tower of London, the queen besieged
stops.campa: Mordred, left as regent, forges letters from beyond the sea saying Arthur is slain, has himself crowned, and takes Guinevere at Winchester, saying plainly he will wed his uncle's wife. She is passing heavy but dares not discover her heart: she speaks fair, agrees to his will, and asks leave to go to London to buy all that a wedding needs. Because of her fair speech he trusts her and lets her go. The moment she is in the city she takes the Tower, stuffs it with victual, garrisons it with men, and answers every summons with silence and the walls.
stops.quote: she stuffed it with all manner of victual, and well garnished it with men, and so kept it
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, ch. 1
suggested_refs: The White Tower, oldest surviving keep of the Tower of London
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, ch. 1

stops.name: Salisbury Plain, the last field
stops.campa: Arthur returns from Gaul, drives Mordred back through Dover and Barham Down, and the two armies meet at last on Salisbury Plain for a parley that a drawn adder ruins: a knight bares his sword against the snake at his heel, both sides read it as treachery, and the field the two kings meant to settle by talk is settled by every weapon they own. Mordred falls on Arthur's own spear; Arthur takes his death-wound in the same stroke. Guinevere is not on the field, but the war that empties it is the one her flight to the Tower helped provoke and could not stop.
suggested_refs: Salisbury Plain
Slaughterbridge stone near Camelford, Cornwall, the rival West Country site of Camlann
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, ch. 4
Annales Cambriae, s.a. 537

stops.name: Amesbury Priory, abbess and penitent
stops.campa: Guinevere hears of Arthur's end and does not wait for Lancelot, who she knows will come. She steals away with five ladies to Amesbury and lets make herself a nun, wearing white clothes and black, living in fasting, prayers and alms-deeds until the house marvels at how virtuously she is changed, and there she is abbess and ruler as reason would. When Lancelot finds her at last she will not let him near, laying the war and the deaths of the noblest knights in the world at the door of their old love, and asking only that he never look on her face again.
stops.quote: Through this man and me hath all this war been wrought, and the death of the most noblest knights of the world... I require thee and beseech thee heartily, for all the love that ever was betwixt us, that thou never see me more in the visage.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, ch. 9
suggested_refs: Amesbury Abbey House, on the site of the medieval priory of the Order of Fontevraud
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, ch. 7 and ch. 9
Amesbury Priory, house of the Order of Fontevraud (refounded 1177)

stops.name: Amesbury, the death and the road to Glastonbury
stops.campa: Lancelot is charged in a vision to ride for Amesbury and comes too late by half an hour: Guinevere has died in her habit, penitent to the last, having prayed for two days that she might never see him again with her worldly eyes. He and his eight fellows carry her body the thirty miles back to Glastonbury on foot, a hundred torches burning around the bier the whole way, and there the monks wrap her in cered cloth of Raines and a web of lead and set her in a coffin of marble beside the husband she outlived by less than a year.
stops.quote: with an hundred torches ever brenning about the corpse of the queen... Thus Sir Launcelot and his eight fellows went on foot from Almesbury unto Glastonbury.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, ch. 11
suggested_refs: Glastonbury Abbey, the site of the medieval high altar where the grave was said to lie
sources: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, ch. 11

stops.name: Glastonbury Abbey, the monks' exhumation
stops.campa: More than six centuries after the burial the monks of Glastonbury, digging in the old cemetery between two ancient pyramids at Abbot Henry de Sully's direction, strike a hollowed oak trunk sixteen feet down. Inside lie the bones of a very tall man, the skull marked by old wounds, and beside him a woman's bones with a tress of golden hair that a monk lifts out whole and that crumbles to dust the moment it is touched. Under a stone above the coffin lies a leaden cross, and cut into its face, in letters turned inward toward the stone, a name six hundred years old surfaces again.
stops.quote: Here lies buried the renowned King Arthur, with Guinevere his second wife, in the Isle of Avalon.
stops.quote_source: The leaden cross, as transcribed by Gerald of Wales, De Principis Instructione (c. 1193)
suggested_refs: The 'King Arthur's Tomb' marker in the ruined choir of Glastonbury Abbey
William Camden's 1607 engraving of the leaden cross, Britannia
sources: Gerald of Wales, De Principis Instructione, Distinctio I, ch. 20
Gerald of Wales, Speculum Ecclesiae
Adam of Domerham, Historia de Rebus Glastoniensibus

segments.name: The Scottish Counter-Tradition: Vanora at Meigle

stops.name: Barry Hill, Vanora's captivity
stops.campa: North of the Roman roads, where the legend keeps its own chronology, the story is told differently and just as certainly. Here the queen is Vanora. Arthur goes on pilgrimage to Rome and leaves his nephew Mordred to rule in his place; Mordred seizes the throne and his uncle's wife, and the two reign together with Pictish troops to enforce it. When Arthur returns and puts his nephew down, the battle does not clear the queen. Vanora is carried to the vitrified ramparts of the fort on Barry Hill above Alyth and held there while she is judged, guilty of treason and of adultery both.
suggested_refs: Barry Hill hillfort ramparts above Alyth, Perthshire
sources: Hector Boece, Scotorum Historia (1527), for the queen carried north by the Picts and buried at Meigle
Local Perthshire tradition of Vanora, Cateran Ecomuseum, 'Barry Hill Fort'
Canmore/Trove.scot site 31061, Barry Hill (vitrified timber-laced rampart)

stops.name: Meigle, Vanora's Mound and the Pictish stones
stops.campa: Arthur's sentence on the woman he no longer calls his queen is to be torn to pieces by a pack of wild dogs, and the local telling carries out the punishment at Meigle, in the heart of Pictish Angus, far from any Avalon in the south. The grass-covered tumulus beside the church becomes Vanora's Mound, her grave, and the carved stones that once stood at its edge, moved now into the village museum, are read by the countryside as her monument: a beast-hunt cut into cross-slab stone, taken by the church for Daniel among the lions, kept by the parish as the queen's own gravestone.
suggested_refs: Meigle 2, the Pictish cross-slab called locally the 'Vanora Stone', in Meigle Sculptured Stone Museum
Vanora's Mound, the tumulus in Meigle churchyard
sources: Hector Boece, Scotorum Historia (1527)
Historic Environment Scotland, Meigle Sculptured Stone Museum
Local Perthshire tradition of Vanora, Cateran Ecomuseum, 'Vanora's Mound'

segments.name: Geoffrey's Ending: York and the Veil of Julius

stops.name: York, the queen in the usurper's north
stops.campa: In the oldest full telling there is no Amesbury and no Glastonbury. Mordred, left as regent, takes the crown and takes the queen, and keeps his court in the north while Arthur is still overseas. Guinevere holds state at York as wife to the man who has usurped her husband; whether by her consent or against it, the History declines to say, and that silence is the whole of her guilt or her innocence. Then Arthur lands at Richborough, Gawain falls on the beach, Mordred is driven out of Winchester and runs west into Cornwall. The news comes north.
suggested_refs: York Minster, raised over the Roman principia of Eboracum, Geoffrey's northern seat
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book X, ch. 13 and Book XI, ch. 1
Aaron Thompson translation, Six Old English Chronicles

stops.name: Caerleon, the veil among the nuns of Julius the Martyr
stops.campa: Despairing of success, she goes from York to the City of the Legions, where the church of Julius the Martyr keeps a choir of virgins vowed to God, and there she takes their habit and their rule. Geoffrey gives her no deathbed, no hundred torches, no marble coffin beside Arthur, no leaden cross surfacing six centuries later. He gives her a door closing on a woman who chooses chastity and silence while the last battle is still being fought somewhere to the south, and then he stops writing about her altogether. It is the same city where she was crowned apart.
stops.quote: As soon as queen Guanhumara heard this, she immediately, despairing of success, fled from York to the City of Legions, where she resolved to live a chaste life among the nuns in the church of Julius the Martyr, and entered herself one of their order.
stops.quote_source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book XI, ch. 1, trans. Aaron Thompson
suggested_refs: The site of the church of Julius the Martyr at Caerleon, one of the two Caerleon martyr-churches named by Gildas and Bede
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book XI, ch. 1
Aaron Thompson translation, Six Old English Chronicles (Wikisource)
Gildas, De Excidio, and Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica I.7 (Julius and Aaron of Caerleon)
